source.title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales

accepted.question_text: What larger, conflict-free framework can reconcile massive-star theory and observations across individual stars, interacting systems, stellar winds, compact-object environments, star clusters, and integrated star-forming galaxies? The framework must explain why some current descriptions conflict across subfields, such as stellar-wind clumps needing to be tiny in spectral modeling but large in X-ray accretion variability, and why single-star evolution models can reproduce integrated star-forming galaxies even though massive stars have high multiplicity and many individual stars and systems are not reproduced by current models.

evidence.quote: Especially when moving accross traditional field boundaries, we find both conflicting descriptions as well as unphysical but strangely “sufficient” treaments. A prominent example for the former are the sizes of clumps in stellar winds, which should be tiny to explain the overall constant appearance of a stellar spectrum, but huge when accreted onto a compact object nearby to explain X-ray lightcurve variations. On larger scales, single star evolution modelling seems to be remarkably sufficient to reproduce the appearance of star-forming galaxies despite the high multiplicity fraction in the massive star regime and the failure to reproduce many observed individual stars and systems.

Trying to resolve these conflicting results quickly leads back to questioning basics we thought to be settled. Hence, what might sound like a problem in the details at first actually hints at big open questions and the search for larger, conflict-free framework for massive stars which is much needed, but so far missing.

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism explains why some high-redshift, star-forming galaxies observed with JWST are strongly enriched in nitrogen relative to oxygen and lie between the carbon-nitrogen and carbon-nitrogen-oxygen equilibrium abundance patterns? Candidate explanations to distinguish include unusually efficient and bursty star formation, dense progenitor systems of globular clusters, enrichment sparked by extremely massive or supermassive stars, enrichment by ordinary massive and very massive stars, and systematic problems in abundance diagnostics, stellar-evolution models, or feedback models, especially because high-redshift metallicity measurements are mostly oxygen-based whereas population-synthesis assumptions about stellar evolution depend strongly on iron abundance.

evidence.quote: Yet, the spectra obtained from star-forming galaxies have led to multiple puzzling discoveries that do not fit in our (previous) view about massive stars, most prominently reionization-era galaxies highly enriched in nitrogen (N). Fig. 1 shows a sample of these objects in the N versus oxygen (O) plane. The galaxies are significantly more N-rich than most known star-forming galaxies and H II regions, but all targets essentially are located between the CN and CNO equilibrium which could be reached even if the galaxies are normal in C/O.

Lots of open questions around these findings are currently discussed (e.g., Cameron et al. 2023; Marques-Chaves et al. 2024; Berg et al. 2025; Arellano-Córdova et al. 2025; Morel et al. 2025): Could more efficient and bursty star-formation be responsible? As the high-redshift galaxies are extremely dense, do we maybe see the progenitors of Globular Clusters, possibly sparked by extremely massive stars or even supermassive stars? Or are massive and very massive stars sufficient and the problem in our understanding is rather located in the diagnostics and well as the evolution and feedback models?

In particular the latter is not getting easier by the fact that metallicity measurements at high redshift are essentially all O-based, while population synthesis models include assumptions about stellar evolution that are significantly depending on the iron abundance.

accepted.question_text: What sources produce the highly ionized environments observed in many low-metallicity and high-redshift galaxies, including nebular helium-ionizing radiation? The answer must determine whether hot Wolf-Rayet stars with comparatively weaker winds, chemically homogeneous-evolution products, Population III stars, or other massive-star channels can supply the necessary hard ionizing flux under the metallicity and evolutionary conditions of those galaxies.

evidence.quote: In parallel, signatures of highly ionized environments are also found in many low-metallicity and high-redshift galaxies. While their origin is still quite unclear, some possible sources are listed in Table 2 and will be discussed further below.

The WN3h stars and the direct WN/WO transition show that WR stars can be strong sources of He II ionizing flux throughout at least a significant part of their He-burning lifetime. This makes them very interesting sources in the context of observed nebular He II emission in lower-metallicity galaxies across a wide redshift range.

The comparison shows that in principle hot WRs with comparably weaker winds could yield the necessary hard ionizing flux. Yet, current evolution and population synthesis models essentially cannot reproduce the observed WN2 and WN3h stars, in particular as most of them do not have a companion.

accepted.question_text: How can high-redshift massive-star observations, which are limited in spatial resolution and wavelength coverage, be robustly connected to the underlying physical processes using a ladder of local analogs and testbed environments? The needed program must link nearby low-metallicity dwarf galaxies, unresolved and resolved clusters, and individual stellar systems, so that detailed stellar physics and population-synthesis constraints can be tied back to integrated high-redshift observations.

evidence.quote: While yielding fascinating new discoveries, high-redshift observations alone will be insufficient to answer any of these questions robustly as the resolution and wavelength regimes are quite limited. A whole ladder of local analogs and testbed environments is required to study and connect the involved physical processes, ranging from nearby (dwarf) galaxies with lower Z over unresolved and resolved clusters to individual stellar systems such as the iron-poor O stars in the Magellanic Bridge (Schösser et al. 2025).

Resolved clusters are a particular important step as individual stars can be studied in detail while the cluster environment yields additional constraints and provides a testbed for population synthesis.

accepted.question_text: How much do unresolved multiplicity and post-interaction binaries distort the inferred properties of massive stars and the interpretation of massive-star populations? A complete answer must determine when objects that appear single from photometry or spectral-type calibrations are actually binary-evolution products such as stripped stars or helium-burning O stars, and how such hidden systems bias stellar temperatures, masses, evolutionary states, and population-synthesis conclusions.

evidence.quote: Within clusters or in the field, resolving and understanding the multiplicity of massive stars is crucial to avoid misinterpretations and solution degeneracities. This requires to go beyond photometry-based studies and ideally multi-epoch spectroscopy to quanitatively analyse the components.

The inferred values from photometry or spectral-type calibrations change drastically when presumably single objects turn out to be post-interaction binaries, implying that our interpretations of less-studied objects can be significantly blurred. The examples further show that long-predicted binary-evolution products (e.g., intermediate-mass stripped stars, He-burning O stars) actually “hide” in what one might consider the “known” OB population.

accepted.question_text: For hot massive stars whose mass-loss rates inferred from standard ultraviolet and optical diagnostics are lower than what radiation pressure could theoretically drive, is the weak-wind problem a failure of radiation-driven wind physics or primarily a diagnostic problem caused by missing wind phases? The question requires distinguishing genuinely weak winds expected in low-density or low-luminosity regimes from cases where the real mass-loss rate is higher because a substantial hot wind component is invisible to standard ultraviolet and optical diagnostics.

evidence.quote: As the associated measured mass-loss rates Ṁ are lower than what is predicted by certain mass-loss predictions, this is also labelled as the weak-wind problem. However, many Ṁ-predictions are based on extrapolating a set of explicit model calculations and thus it is by no means clear whether the insufficiency of a prediction also indicates an actual problem in our physical understanding of radiation-driven winds.
Instead, the weak-wind problem in its actual meaning deals with stars where Ṁ derived from standard UV and optical diagnostics is lower than what could theoretically be driven by radiation pressure.

For the Galactic case of μ Col, Huenemoerder et al. (2012) presented the intriguing solution that the winds of the stars subjected to weak-wind problem might rather be the problem of a multi-phased wind and missing diagnostics. From X-ray spectroscopy, they derived a six-times higher Ṁ, concluding that a significant fraction of the wind is in a hot phase, invisible to the UV and optical diagnostics.

accepted.question_text: Why do the two nearby O9-type dwarf stars 10 Lac and μ Col require different wind diagnostics, and how regime-dependent is the presence of a hot wind component in weak-wind stars? The problem includes determining whether the hot phase is sometimes only the tail of a wind-structure distribution, whether it can become the dominant wind component in stars subject to the weak-wind problem, and whether the transition between these regimes is smooth.
accepted.context_brief: Regime dependence of hot wind phases

evidence.quote: Recently, this idea got new support from JWST mid-IR observations of the nearby O9 dwarf 10 Lac, where forbidden high-ionization fine-structure emission lines indicate a ten-times higher Ṁ (Law et al. 2024). Notably, these lines are not visible in the JWST mid-IR spectrum of μ Col, raising the question why two stars with very similar spectral types require so different diagnostics.

Nonetheless, more observational guidance would be extremely helpful as it is so far unclear how regime-dependent the presence of a hotter wind component is and whether there is a smooth transition from the hot phase actually being a tail of a distribution to presumably becoming a dominant component in stars subjected to the “weak-wind problem”.

accepted.question_text: How should Wolf-Rayet spectral classifications be mapped to the underlying stellar structures, evolutionary states, and feedback properties of Wolf-Rayet stars? The answer must account for the fact that the same WN, WC, or WO subtype label can be produced by line ratios with different absolute line strengths, kinetic feedback, hydrostatic radii, hydrogen content, and burning stages, so treating Wolf-Rayet stars as one homogeneous group can misrepresent both evolution and feedback.

evidence.quote: However, this does not apply to all WR stars and the treatment of WR stars as one big homogeneous group is another example, where a blurred perception can have striking consequences. The spectral classification into WN, WC, and WO with further subtypes defined by line ratios provides a first distinction, but the association with both evolution and feedback is tricky.

As the ratio of two strong lines can be the same as the ratio of two weaker lines, objects with very different kinetic feedback as well as different hydrostatic radii can appear under the same label. The association with stellar structure and evolution through the subtypes is therefore non-trivial with many pitfalls.

Strong constraints exist for WC and WO stars, which never show hydrogen (H) in their spectra and thus have to be He-burning (“classical”) WR (cWR) stars. WN stars instead can either be H- or He-burning, unless their outer layers are (almost) depleted in H.

accepted.question_text: What evolutionary pathways form the observed bulk population of Wolf-Rayet stars whose current structures or formation routes are not explained by standard evolutionary predictions? The problem includes determining the roles of intrinsic mass loss, luminous-blue-variable envelope loss and giant eruptions, binary interaction, and possible short-lived stripping phases in producing lower-luminosity strong-wind Wolf-Rayet subtypes such as the WN5–7 and WC8–9 populations seen in Westerlund 1.
accepted.context_brief: Formation channels of observed Wolf-Rayet populations

evidence.quote: However, the association with the observed population remains challenging. The bulk of the known WR population actually consists of objects where either the current structure is not in line with evolutionary predictions or the pathway to forming these WR stars is totally unclear.

The loss of the envelope, in particular below the VMS regime, is a classic explanation in massive single-star evolution (Langer et al. 1994). However, the association of LBVs and in particular giant eruptions as an outcome of the single-star evolution is debated (e.g. Mehner et al. 2021; Smith 2026). Indeed, binarity is common among WR stars, although this does not imply that binary interaction is always the (main) cause for reaching the observed configurations (e.g. Shenar et al. 2020).

Yet, binary interaction might be an important route to produce certain WR subtypes with strong winds at comparably lower luminosities. For example, the WR population of Wd1 contains mostly WN5-7 and WC8-9 stars with dust excess and X-ray luminosities suggesting all of them to be binaries (Crowther et al. 2006; Anastasopoulou et al. 2024).

accepted.question_text: Are supergiant B[e] stars a missing evolutionary link in the formation of mid-type WN Wolf-Rayet binaries, by masking post-common-envelope systems behind circumstellar material? This question includes testing whether objects such as HD 38489 in the Large Magellanic Cloud and Wd1-9 in Westerlund 1 hide Wolf-Rayet plus OB-star binary configurations beneath B[e]-type spectra or circumstellar emission.
accepted.context_brief: sgB[e] stars as hidden post-common-envelope systems

evidence.quote: A missing link in the formation of mid-type WN binaries could be sgB[e] stars, masking post-common envelope systems. In the LMC, the sgB[e] HD 38489 (aka LHA 120-S134) shows broad He II 4686 Å-emission within a B[e]-type spectrum (e.g, Massey et al. 2014) and many authors conclude that the B[e] phenomenon does not reflect the underlying object(s), but only shows the circumstellar material (e.g., Zickgraf et al. 1986; Clark et al. 2013).
Intestingly, the X-ray spectrum of the sgB[e] Wd1-9 also indicates a WR+OB binary (Anastasopoulou et al. 2025).

accepted.question_text: How do transition layers and mixing above the convective helium core shape the WN-to-WC and WN-to-WO evolutionary stages of hydrogen-free Wolf-Rayet stars? The problem is to explain why observed WN/WC transition stars, nitrogen-bearing WC stars, and WN/WO transition objects have intermediate spectral features and surface abundances, including WN/WO oxygen abundances lower than carbon abundances, even though the WN-to-WC transition is commonly predicted to be extremely fast.

evidence.quote: The transition from a WN to a WC stage is commonly predicted to be extremely fast. However, a small but notable population of WN/WC-transition stars as well as WC stars with remaining nitrogen indicate that a considerable transition layer is typical, pointing at a considerable mixing above the convective He core (Langer 1991).

Sander et al. (2025) could show that this object is in fact in a WN-to-WO transition with another WN/WO star found in M33. This stage marks a hotter counterpart of the aforementioned WN/WC stage, happening when the wind mass-loss rates are insufficient to considerably cloak the hotter wind-launching layers. Yet, the oxygen abundances of WN/WO stars are considerably lower than their carbon abundances, in line with what was found in a recent investigation of LMC WO stars by Aadland et al. (2022).

accepted.question_text: How can stellar-evolution and population-synthesis models reproduce observed WN2 and WN3h Wolf-Rayet stars, especially cases with no detectable companion, while also accounting for their role as strong helium-ionizing sources? A successful answer must explain the formation of early-type WN stars in subsolar-metallicity environments, the absence of plausible dark massive companions for the Small Magellanic Cloud WN3 stars, and the hard ionizing flux that such stars may contribute to low-metallicity galaxies.
accepted.context_brief: Formation of WN2 and WN3h helium-ionizing sources

evidence.quote: While the WN3 stars in the SMC all contain at least some hydrogen, the even hotter WN2 type can be found in the outer regions of the Milky Way, M33, and the LMC, likely also being connected to subsolar metallicity.
The WN3h stars and the direct WN/WO transition show that WR stars can be strong sources of He II ionizing flux throughout at least a significant part of their He-burning lifetime.

Yet, current evolution and population synthesis models essentially cannot reproduce the observed WN2 and WN3h stars, in particular as most of them do not have a companion. For the SMC WN3 stars, a detailed multi-epoch monitoring actually also ruled out essentially all plausible dark massive companions (Schootemeijer et al. 2024), leaving another open question in massive star research.

accepted.question_text: How can resolved observations of individual massive stars and clusters be connected to integrated-light observations so that population synthesis correctly maps detailed stellar physics into galaxy-scale predictions? The answer requires determining what multi-epoch spectroscopy, ultraviolet diagnostics, and future facilities such as the Extremely Large Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory must measure to close remaining knowledge gaps in massive-star multiplicity, binary-interaction outcomes, stellar feedback, and integrated population modeling.

evidence.quote: Spectroscopic observations, ideally multi-epoch, are the key to get proper answers, in particular as multiplicity is almost everywhere, but aquiring this data for large samples remains an ongoing challenge. The UV marks a particularly crucial regime here as it bears unique diagnostics for many decisive outcomes of binary interaction.

Connecting resolved and integrated observations of massive stars is challenging, but essential for a coherent understanding of massive stars and to ensure population synthesis correctly maps the insights from resolved populations. This is particularly crucial as many regimes will remain limited to integrated-light studies.

To close knowledge gaps, forthcoming facilities such the ELT or eventually the Habitable World Observatory can become gamechangers, but need to be designed with massive stars in mind to provide the necessary senstivitiy and diagnostics.
